title: Can an AI tutor teach as well as a human? Recalculating StudentBench equivalence tests
description: Recalculating 38 equivalence tests from 19 published StudentBench contrasts, with implications for measuring human outcomes in Anicca.

attribution.text: Anicca Research. Public aggregate reanalysis; no new human study or model training.

markdown:
# Can an AI tutor teach as well as a human? Recalculating StudentBench equivalence tests

An AI solving a problem and a student learning to solve that problem are different outcomes. The distinction matters for Anicca, whose objective is to help people pursue their own goals without creating unnecessary dependence on an assistant.

**Finding.** We recalculated 38 two one-sided tests (TOST) from 19 published StudentBench contrast estimates. All matched the released numerical targets. The adjusted pooled AI-minus-human difference is −0.577 percentage points (90% confidence interval −2.180 to +1.026; equivalence p=0.0152 at a ±4.085-point margin). The verbal section alone does not meet that criterion. These are results from the authors' published human study, not evidence that Anicca's Manager can teach as effectively as a human.

![Cover: 2,469 sessions, 19 estimates and 38 recalculated tests](/assets/research/studentbench-h25-cover.svg)

## The outcome that matters

Imagine a student unable to multiply two numbers. A tutor can provide the answer in one turn, or help the student find a strategy. Both may produce a correct answer during the conversation. Only a subsequent assessment without help can tell us whether the student learned. The same problem arises in a behavior-change product: opening a notification is not evidence of improved well-being or independence.

[StudentBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28470) reports a GRE tutoring study conducted in summer 2026. There were 2,383 participants and 2,469 completed section sessions. Each session involved a 27-question pretest, one hour of the assigned intervention, and a 27-question posttest. The study included AI tutoring, human tutoring and no-tutor conditions. A separate study obtained 2,028 pairwise evaluations from 51 expert tutors. These assessments distinguish teaching quality during an interaction from unaided learning outcomes.

![Figure 1. Pretest, intervention, unaided posttest and equivalence assessment](/assets/research/studentbench-h25-design.svg)

Figure 1 is a conceptual representation of the published study. It does not imply that we performed random assignment or a delayed follow-up ourselves. Source: original paper and dataset card.

## Equivalence is not an insignificant difference

A conventional difference test asks whether we can reject a null difference of zero. Failure to reject may simply mean that estimates are too imprecise. An equivalence test asks whether the entire plausible difference is small enough to be practically acceptable.

Let d be the AI-minus-human effect difference, Δ a predeclared equivalence margin, e the estimate, s its standard error and ν its degrees of freedom. The two null hypotheses are d ≤ −Δ and d ≥ Δ. Reject both to establish equivalence at the chosen significance level. With a Student t reference distribution, the TOST p-value is the maximum of the upper tail at (e+Δ)/s and the lower tail at (e−Δ)/s. At a 5% significance level, equivalence corresponds to a 90% confidence interval lying entirely within the two margins.

The margin matters. A wide margin can hide a practically meaningful decline. A narrow one demands more precise evidence. We retained the published margins of 0.20 and 0.25 pooled standard deviations and did not tune them to obtain significance.

## What we actually ran

We obtained the published comparison targets from the official repository at revision a3c0e638a6a9d76c42cdcb633781f2a392aefa3e and aggregate tables from the dataset at revision 304c8d63c726e72b60510bba3a44454fc0726721. The data card identifies a CC BY 4.0 license and explicitly asks researchers to keep benchmark data out of training corpora. We downloaded no individual learner responses, transcripts or identifiers.

Our audit reads the estimates, standard errors, degrees of freedom and margins, then calculates confidence intervals and TOST probabilities with SciPy. A second calculation uses the incomplete beta function for the t-distribution CDF. We also verify that the confidence-interval containment criterion matches the test decision. All 38 tests and all 19 pairs of 90% and 95% intervals match the published targets within the recorded numerical tolerances. Normal and optimized Python produced byte-identical receipts.

This is an aggregate numerical audit, not an independent refit of the original regressions. The primary equivalence implementation uses cluster-robust CR2 variance and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; its original row fingerprints and dependency structure remain to be validated in a full reproduction.

## The pooled result does not apply to every section

![Figure 2. Recomputed 90% confidence intervals and equivalence margins](/assets/research/studentbench-h25-ci.svg)

Figure 2. Adjusted AI-minus-human contrasts. Combined n=2,279; quant n=1,200; verbal n=1,079. Shaded intervals show the 0.25 pooled-SD margins. The estimates, SEs and degrees of freedom are from the official comparison targets, not a newly collected experiment.

| Scope | Sessions | Difference (pp) | 90% CI | Margin (pp) | TOST p | Equivalent? |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| Combined | 2,279 | −0.577 | [−2.180, 1.026] | ±4.085 | 0.0152 | Yes |
| Quantitative | 1,200 | +0.877 | [−1.804, 3.558] | ±4.140 | 0.0279 | Yes |
| Verbal | 1,079 | −2.194 | [−4.314, −0.073] | ±3.895 | 0.0851 | Not established |

At the narrower 0.20-SD margin, the quantitative comparison has p=0.0640 and also fails to establish equivalence. The verbal result is not proof of inferiority. It is insufficient evidence for equivalence within the selected bounds. Reporting only a pooled p-value would obscure this important distinction.

## Dependence matters more than the apparent sample size

The released overlap table contains 1,205 people who completed only quantitative, 86 who completed both sections, and 1,092 who completed only verbal. These sum to 2,383 people; adding the second session of each of the 86 repeat participants gives 2,469 sessions. Treating sessions as distinct people would inflate the independent sample size. Human tutors also teach multiple students. The pooled adjusted analysis accounts for such dependencies; its published effective degrees of freedom are only 1.591.

A separate collection-cohort aggregate contains 1,796 AI sessions with a mean gain of 13.856 points and 140 human sessions with a mean gain of 15.608 points. The raw difference is −1.753 points. This differs from the adjusted pooled estimate because the cohort and analysis differ. It is descriptive and cannot replace the study's adjusted contrast or establish a causal effect.

The released robustness-grid counts contain 4,474 planned definitions, 2,694 unique groups and 1,780 duplicate definitions; 330 unique groups were eligible and 2,364 ineligible. We checked those accounting identities, not the 330 regressions. For the 13 reported leave-one-human-tutor-out contrasts, we recalculated the wider-margin TOST and all 13 met the equivalence criterion. This is a check of the released estimates, not a rerun of the omitted-cohort fits.

## Designing an evaluation for Anicca

Manager's ability to predict what people do, the mobile app's ability to alter an immediate action, and long-term benefit are three separate claims. A behavior intervention should have an outcome chosen by the person, a predeclared meaningful difference, independent measurement, a dependency-aware analysis, and explicit records of burden, adverse outcomes and missing data. For example, an evaluation of waking interventions could measure whether users reach their chosen waking goal after prompts are gradually reduced, not merely how often a notification is tapped.

That is a proposed measurement design, not a deployed feature or a claim of benefit. No Manager training or inference occurred in this audit. The study concerns immediate GRE outcomes, not delayed retention or universal teaching efficacy. Its groups and pricing assumptions limit what can be inferred about other products. We will not use evaluation data to train a model or conflate a simulated learner with a real person.

The next empirical step is to reproduce the original fits using permitted data and the official harness. For a system intended to improve people's lives, the appropriate north star is an independently measured human outcome, not merely an impressive AI response.
